title: Approximating Area with Rectangles
short: Add up rectangle areas to estimate the area under a curve.
trouble: Students use the wrong endpoints for left and right sums.

blocks.html: How much area lies under a curve? For rectangles and triangles we have formulas; for a curved boundary we do not. The plan: cover the region with thin rectangles and add their areas. Sigma Notation keeps the sums tidy, and limits will later make them exact.

Split $[a, b]$ into $n$ equal strips of width $\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$, with endpoints $x_i = a + i\,\Delta x$. The left sum uses the heights at the left ends, $L_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(x_i)\,\Delta x$; the right sum uses the right ends, $R_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i)\,\Delta x$.

blocks.name: riemann

opts.task: Switch between left and right, then raise $n$. Which sum is too small for this rising curve?

blocks.cap: Left and right sums for $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 2]$. The exact area is $\frac{8}{3} \approx 2.667$.

blocks.html: Each rectangle's area is height times width, $f(x_i)\,\Delta x$. Over a thin strip the curve barely changes, so the rectangle is close to the true slice of area. Thinner strips make the error smaller. For a rising curve, left heights are the lowest point of each strip (an underestimate) and right heights are the highest (an overestimate), so the true area is trapped between them.

blocks.title: Left and right sums
blocks.q: Estimate the area under $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 2]$ with $n = 4$, using left and right endpoints.
blocks.a: $L_4 = 1.75$ and $R_4 = 3.75$. The true area, $\frac{8}{3}$, lies between them.

blocks.title: From data
blocks.q: A car's speed is recorded every 10 seconds: 20, 26, 30, 31, 33 ft/s at $t = 0, 10, 20, 30, 40$. Estimate the distance traveled with a left sum.
steps: Distance = area under the speed graph. Width 10 s.
Left endpoints use the first four readings: $10\,(20 + 26 + 30 + 31) = 10 \cdot 107 = 1070$.
blocks.a: About 1070 ft (the right sum, 1200 ft, gives an upper estimate here).

blocks.html: Using the wrong endpoints, for example all five readings, or starting the right sum at $x = a$. Left sums use $x_0$ through $x_{n-1}$; right sums use $x_1$ through $x_n$. Check: count your heights. There must be exactly $n$ of them, one per strip.
